title: Reading Between the Lines
blurb: Guess the meaning of new words from context

steps.html:
On one Spanish island, a conversation can cross a valley without a single word being spoken. Two texts, a set of verbs that insist on their own preposition, and a way of dealing with words you have never seen.

  • Work out the meaning of new words from the text around them
  • Use consist of, contribute to, adapt to, result in and others
  • Write a short description of a way of communicating

steps.title: Which of these could carry a full message over a long distance?
steps.sub: Choose any you think would work.

steps.title: Before you read.
steps.prompt: A whistled language would most likely develop in a place where…
options: people live very close together in a small town
deep valleys make short distances slow to cross
the weather is too loud for ordinary speech
steps.answer: deep valleys make short distances slow to cross
steps.why: Whistling carries much further than the voice, which matters when two villages are minutes apart by sight and an hour apart on foot.

steps.title: Study the words.
steps.sub: Six of them are verbs that always take the same preposition. Learn the two together.

words.def: To be made up of the parts named. Never used in the continuous.
To be one of the causes of something, or to help make it happen.
To change so that you fit a new situation.
To think that something is wrong or bad.
To know that someone or something exists, without knowing much more.
To cause something to happen as a direct consequence.
To make a high sound by forcing air through your lips.
The musical sound that birds make.
A person who lives on an island.
A deep, narrow valley with steep sides.
Rising or falling sharply, so that climbing is hard work.
A mountain with an opening through which hot rock is forced out.
A small four-stringed instrument, held like a very small guitar.
So unusual or remarkable that it surprises you.
An act of trying to do something, especially something difficult.
A very long time. Informal, and always plural in this meaning.

steps.title: The island that talks across the valleys
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 141 words

La Gomera is one of the smallest of the Canary Islands, and from the sea it looks like the tip of a volcano pushed up out of the water. Deep ravines cut through it, and the steep hills mean that two villages can face each other across a valley and still be an hour's walk apart.

That geography contributed to something extraordinary. Islanders learned to whistle their language across the ravines. Silbo Gomero consists of four vowels and four consonants, and a good whistler can be understood three kilometres away. Visitors who hear it for the first time often confuse it with birdsong.

The language adapted to Spanish when Spanish arrived, and it has survived every change since. Older islanders still disapprove of the idea that Silbo is finished. The arrival of the mobile phone resulted in a sharp decline, but not in silence.

steps.title: Which heading best fits the text?
options: A language shaped by the land it grew in
How tourism destroyed a local language
steps.answer: A language shaped by the land it grew in
steps.why: The geography — ravines, steep hills, distance — is what the whole text hangs on.

steps.title: Whistling in the playground
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 138 words

Had you heard of Silbo Gomero before this page? Most people have not. For ages it was treated as a language for farmers rather than for schools, and by 1990 hardly anyone under thirty could whistle a full sentence.

Then the island made an attempt to save it. Since 1999 every child on La Gomera has studied Silbo at school. The lessons consist of listening, imitating, and eventually whistling messages from one side of a playground to the other. Teachers say the children adapt to it far faster than adults do.

Isidro Ortiz, who teaches it, is relaxed about what the language becomes. 'A language adapts to the people who use it,' he says. 'My students whistle about football. One of them whistled a ukulele tune at me last week. If that contributes to keeping it alive, I do not disapprove of it at all.'

steps.title: Why the preposition is not optional
steps.html:
A recycled area. The full picture first, then a long example bank.

Some verbs are followed by a fixed preposition. The preposition is not chosen by meaning — it belongs to the verb, and there is usually no rule to work it out from. Learn the verb and its preposition as one item.

After these prepositions, a verb takes -ing, never the infinitive: She apologised for being late. — not for to be late.

Some verbs take a different preposition with a different meaning: hear of = know that something exists; hear about = get news of it; hear from = receive a message from someone.

A few verbs take an object first: adapt something to something — The locals adapted the language to Spanish.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences. Cover the right-hand half and test yourself.

The course consists of twelve units.
Never consists in in this meaning, and never continuous.

Poor planning contributed to the delay.
One cause among several.

The delay resulted in a formal complaint.
A direct consequence.

Older islanders disapprove of the idea.
Of, not with.

Have you heard of her?
= Do you know she exists?

Have you heard from her?
= Has she been in touch?

Children adapt to change quickly.
To, not with.

They adapted the language to Spanish.
Object first, then the preposition.

Everything depends on the weather.
On, not from.

She apologised for interrupting me.
-ing after the preposition.

They succeeded in saving the language.
-ing again.

Who does this ukulele belong to?
The preposition stays at the end of the question.

steps.title: Building a sentence around a dependent preposition
steps.html:
1. You want to say that mobile phones were one cause of the decline.
  2. Choose the verb: contribute. Its preposition is fixed: to.
  3. Put the cause first, the preposition next, the result after it: Mobile phones contributed to the decline.
  4. If the result is an action rather than a noun, it must be -ing: Mobile phones contributed to killing the language. — never to kill here.
  5. Compare the stronger verb: result in claims a direct consequence, so Mobile phones resulted in the decline is a bigger claim than contributed to.

steps.title: You are going to describe a way of communicating that is disappearing.
steps.sub: Choose the one you will write about.

options.label: A regional language or dialect near you
A traditional signal — bells, drums, smoke
A craft or skill passed on by speaking, not writing

steps.title: Write your description.
steps.sub: 130–160 words. Use at least four verb + preposition pairs from this lesson.
steps.placeholder: Almost nobody outside … has heard of …
steps.html:
• Say what it is and what it consists of.
  • Explain what contributed to its decline, and what that resulted in.
  • Say how people feel about it now — who approves, who disapproves.
  • Finish with the situation today.

Useful language

  • It consists of …
  • … contributed to its decline.
  • … resulted in …
  • Older speakers disapprove of …
  • Younger people have adapted to …
  • Most people outside the region have never heard of it.
steps.modelHtml:
The whistled shepherds' calls of the mountains

Almost nobody outside the region has heard of them. The system consists of about twenty short calls, each one carrying a single instruction, and it was used by shepherds working on hills too steep to cross quickly.

Two things contributed to its decline. Roads reached the high pastures in the 1970s, and the radio arrived a decade later. Together they resulted in a generation that never needed to learn it.

A few older shepherds still disapprove of the recordings that researchers now make, because a call learned from a machine is not the same as a call learned on a hillside. Their grandchildren have adapted to the recordings anyway. Around forty people can still use the calls, which is thirty-nine more than in 1995.
